title: Breast Zones and Layers
front clue: Skin, fat, gland, fat, muscle: three zones stacked between skin and chest wall
core concept: Sonographically the breast is described from superficial to deep as skin, the premammary (subcutaneous) zone, the mammary zone, and the retromammary zone, with the pectoralis major muscle, ribs, and pleura behind. Normal skin is a bright double line with a thin hypoechoic dermis, generally under 2 mm thick (slightly thicker, up to about 3 mm, near the areola and inframammary fold). The premammary zone holds subcutaneous fat lobules (hypoechoic, mid-gray), Cooper ligaments, veins, and lymphatics. The mammary zone lies between the superficial and deep layers of the superficial fascia and contains the echogenic fibroglandular parenchyma, ducts, and interspersed fat; most breast cancers and fibroadenomas arise here. The retromammary zone is a thin fat layer separating the deep fascia from the pectoralis major, which appears as a striated hypoechoic band. Ribs are oval hypoechoic structures with posterior shadowing deep to the muscle, and costal cartilage can mimic a mass. Tissue composition is reported as homogeneous fat, homogeneous fibroglandular, or heterogeneous.
why it matters: Knowing which zone a lesion lives in narrows the differential fast. A lesion entirely in the skin or subcutaneous fat, such as a sebaceous or epidermal inclusion cyst or a lipoma, is rarely a primary breast cancer, while an irregular mass in the mammary zone deserves full scrutiny. Fat is the gain reference: set the gain so fat is medium gray, not black. Common traps include calling a rib or costal cartilage a mass (trace it into the chest wall and confirm it is deep to the pectoralis) and calling a fat lobule a hypoechoic mass (rotate the probe and watch it elongate and blend with surrounding fat).
on the registry: Expect questions asking which zone contains the glandular tissue or which layer lies directly anterior to the pectoralis major, and items about mistaking ribs or fat lobules for masses.
checkpoint: Pre, mammary, retro: fat, gland, fat, then muscle

title: Cooper Ligaments
front clue: Echogenic suspension cables: straight and thin is normal, pulled or thickened is not
core concept: Cooper ligaments are the suspensory ligaments of the breast: thin connective tissue bands that extend from the deep fascia through the parenchyma and the premammary fat to attach to the dermis. On ultrasound they are thin, curvilinear echogenic lines that outline the fat lobules and arch toward the skin, best seen in the premammary zone. Because they meet the beam at an angle, they can refract sound and produce narrow posterior shadows (critical angle shadowing) that mimic a suspicious lesion; these artifactual shadows disappear with increased compression or a change in transducer angle. Malignancy can thicken, straighten, or retract the ligaments, pulling them toward a mass and causing skin dimpling or retraction. Edema, inflammation, and lymphatic obstruction can also thicken them. With aging and loss of elasticity the ligaments stretch, contributing to breast ptosis. Disruption or interruption of the ligaments by a mass is an associated feature that supports invasion.
why it matters: The reasoning is simple: a real shadowing lesion persists in every plane and with compression, while ligament shadowing comes and goes as you rock the transducer. Exam items often describe a narrow shadow that resolves with pressure and ask for the cause. On the flip side, a desmoplastic carcinoma tethers the ligaments, so a clinical sign of skin dimpling or retraction should send you looking for a mass beneath it. Do not confuse thickened ligaments from edema with tethering: edema thickens many ligaments diffusely and usually comes with skin thickening, whereas retraction is focal and points toward a mass.
on the registry: Tested as the cause of a refractive shadow that disappears with compression, or as the structure responsible for skin retraction over a cancer.
checkpoint: Shadow that vanishes with pressure is a ligament, not a lesion

title: Terminal Ductal Lobular Unit
front clue: The TDLU is the breast's factory and where most breast pathology begins
core concept: Each breast has about 15 to 20 lobes arranged radially around the nipple. Each lobe drains through a lactiferous duct that widens into a lactiferous sinus just beneath the nipple before opening on its surface. Ducts branch peripherally into segmental and subsegmental ducts and end in the terminal ductal lobular unit (TDLU), made of an extralobular terminal duct, an intralobular terminal duct, and the lobule with its acini (ductules). The TDLU is the functional milk-producing unit and the site of origin of most breast pathology: ductal and lobular carcinomas, cysts, fibroadenomas, and fibrocystic change. Ducts are lined by an inner epithelial layer and an outer myoepithelial layer on a basement membrane; in situ cancers stay inside this membrane, invasive cancers breach it. On ultrasound normal ducts are thin anechoic tubes converging on the nipple, most visible in the subareolar region; a duct over about 3 mm in a nonlactating woman is commonly called ectatic. Individual TDLUs are sometimes seen as tiny oval hypoechoic structures.
why it matters: This card ties anatomy to pathology. If the TDLU is where disease starts, then radial scanning along a duct toward the nipple is how you show disease spreading, such as duct extension of carcinoma or an intraductal papilloma within a dilated duct. The basement membrane is the line between in situ and invasive disease, which is why DCIS is stage 0. A common trap is believing that ductal carcinoma arises in large ducts and lobular carcinoma in lobules; both actually arise in the TDLU, and the names describe histologic pattern, not site.
on the registry: Expect recall items naming the TDLU as the origin of most cancers and fibroadenomas, and items on the number of lobes and the lactiferous sinus.
checkpoint: TDLU: where milk is made and where most cancer starts

title: Lymphatic Drainage
front clue: Most lymph heads to the axilla; medial tumors may also drain to internal mammary nodes
core concept: Breast lymph drains mainly to the axillary nodes, which receive roughly 75 percent or more of lymphatic flow, including flow from all quadrants. The remainder travels to the internal mammary (parasternal) chain, particularly from medial and deep tissue, with lesser routes to the interpectoral (Rotter) nodes between the pectoralis major and minor, the supraclavicular and infraclavicular nodes, and occasionally the contralateral breast or the abdomen. The subareolar lymphatic plexus (Sappey plexus) collects lymph from the nipple and areola and connects with deeper channels. Intramammary lymph nodes occur within the breast itself, most often in the upper outer quadrant and axillary tail. The sentinel lymph node is the first node to receive drainage from a tumor and is identified surgically with radiotracer or dye; when it is negative, the rest of the axilla is unlikely to be involved. Blockage of dermal lymphatics by tumor causes skin edema and peau d'orange, the hallmark of inflammatory carcinoma. Normal lymphatic vessels are not usually seen on ultrasound.
why it matters: When you find a cancer, the next question is where it could have spread, so the drainage map tells you where to look. Scan the ipsilateral axilla for every suspicious mass, and remember that medial cancers can skip to the internal mammary chain, which runs along the sternal border and is harder to evaluate. A classic trap is assuming medial lesions drain only medially; the axilla is still the dominant route from every quadrant. Another is forgetting the intramammary node: an oval mass with a fatty hilum in the upper outer quadrant is usually a benign node, not a new tumor.
on the registry: Tested as the primary drainage route (axillary), the destination of medial drainage (internal mammary), and the definition of a sentinel node.
checkpoint: Axilla gets most; internal mammary gets the medial share

title: Physiologic Changes Across Life
front clue: Hormones remodel the breast: bud, cycle, pregnancy, milk, then fat
core concept: At birth, maternal hormones can cause transient neonatal breast enlargement. At puberty (thelarche), estrogen drives ductal elongation and progesterone drives lobular development; the early breast bud appears as a hypoechoic, triangular or disc-shaped retroareolar nodule that must not be biopsied, because removal can prevent breast development. During the menstrual cycle the luteal (premenstrual) phase brings fluid retention, glandular swelling, and tenderness; breast MRI is best scheduled in the second week of the cycle. In pregnancy the glandular tissue proliferates markedly, the fibroglandular zone becomes thick and relatively hypoechoic, and vascularity increases. During lactation prolactin stimulates milk production and oxytocin drives ejection; ultrasound shows prominent, fluid-filled ducts and increased flow. After menopause, falling estrogen causes involution: the glandular tissue atrophies and is replaced by fat, so the breast becomes predominantly fatty with thin echogenic fibrous strands. Hormone replacement therapy can maintain or increase density and may produce new cysts.
why it matters: Many exam scenarios hinge on knowing what is normal for the patient's age and hormonal state. A dense, hypoechoic, vascular breast is expected in a pregnant patient, while a new solid mass in a postmenopausal woman not on hormones is suspicious because new benign hormone-driven lesions such as cysts and fibroadenomas are uncommon then. In a prepubertal girl with a unilateral retroareolar lump, the answer is almost always a normal breast bud. Ultrasound is the preferred first imaging test in pregnant and lactating patients, and lactating breasts should be emptied before scanning when possible.
on the registry: Tested with age-based scenarios: the prepubertal breast bud, the pregnant or lactating breast, and fatty involution after menopause.
checkpoint: Puberty builds, pregnancy multiplies, menopause replaces with fat

title: Normal Variants and Mimics
front clue: Breast tissue can appear anywhere along the milk line from axilla to groin
core concept: The embryologic mammary ridge (milk line) runs from the axilla to the groin, and incomplete regression produces ectopic tissue along it. Polythelia, an accessory nipple, is the most common congenital anomaly, usually found below the normal breast. Polymastia means accessory breast tissue, most often in the axilla, and it can swell during pregnancy and lactation and develop any disease the normal breast can, including cancer; on ultrasound it resembles normal fibroglandular tissue. Amastia (absent breast) and amazia (absent glandular tissue with a nipple present) are rare. Poland syndrome combines unilateral absence or hypoplasia of the pectoralis major with ipsilateral breast hypoplasia. Developmental asymmetry is common and benign when stable. Other normal structures that mimic masses include fat lobules, ribs and costal cartilage, an intramammary lymph node, the nipple itself (which can shadow posteriorly), and dilated subareolar ducts. Tubular breasts and inverted nipples are additional developmental variants.
why it matters: On the exam and in the clinic, the safe question is whether a finding behaves like normal tissue. Accessory axillary tissue looks like glandular tissue and changes with hormones; it is not a mass. Nipple shadowing is eliminated by angling the probe from the side, using more gel, or a standoff pad. A trap: assuming ectopic tissue is immune to disease; it can develop fibroadenomas or carcinoma, so a discrete mass in axillary breast tissue deserves the same workup as one in the breast. Know Poland syndrome by its muscle absence, which helps answer anatomy questions about the chest wall.
on the registry: Expect items on the milk line, the most common congenital anomaly (polythelia), the most common site of accessory tissue (axilla), and Poland syndrome.
checkpoint: Milk line: axilla to groin; accessory tissue can still get cancer

title: Patient Positioning
front clue: Thin the breast: roll the patient and raise the arm
core concept: The goal of positioning is to make the breast as thin and evenly spread over the chest wall as possible, because thinner tissue allows higher frequencies and better resolution. The patient lies supine with the ipsilateral arm raised and the hand behind the head, which stretches the pectoralis and flattens the breast. For the lateral (outer) breast and axillary tail, the patient is rolled into a contralateral posterior oblique position with a wedge or pillow under the ipsilateral shoulder, so the lateral tissue falls medially over the chest wall. For the medial breast, a flat supine position usually suffices. Large or ptotic breasts may need additional rolling and support. Palpable lumps can be scanned in the position in which the patient feels them, while the sonographer palpates the lump and places the transducer directly over it to confirm correlation. Gentle, firm compression reduces thickness, displaces fat, and helps distinguish real masses from tissue folds.
why it matters: Positioning is the cheapest image optimization you have. A breast that is not thinned forces you to lower frequency and widen the focal region, and deep lesions near the chest wall may be missed. Exam questions often ask which position best evaluates the upper outer quadrant or axilla; the answer is the contralateral posterior oblique with the arm raised. A trap is scanning a palpable lump without correlating it under the fingers; always confirm that the sonographic finding is the thing the patient or clinician feels, and document that correlation.
on the registry: Tested as the best position for the lateral breast and axilla, and the reason the arm is raised (to flatten tissue over the chest wall).
checkpoint: Lateral breast: roll away and raise the arm

title: Clock-Face Labeling
front clue: Side, clock time, centimeters from nipple, and scan plane: every image, every time
core concept: Breast lesions are labeled by side (right or left), clock-face position as if the examiner were facing the patient, distance from the nipple in centimeters, and the scan plane (radial or antiradial, or transverse or sagittal). Many protocols also note transducer orientation and depth. On the clock face, 12 o'clock is superior and 6 o'clock inferior for both breasts. Because the clock is read facing the patient, 9 o'clock is lateral on the right breast and 3 o'clock is lateral on the left. The upper outer quadrant therefore spans 9 to 12 o'clock on the right and 12 to 3 o'clock on the left. The subareolar region is labeled retroareolar, and the axilla is labeled separately. Quadrant names (upper outer, upper inner, lower outer, lower inner) are acceptable supplements but less precise. A complete label lets a radiologist, a surgeon, or the next sonographer find the same lesion, correlate it with mammography or MRI, and target it for biopsy.
why it matters: Labeling errors cause wrong-site biopsies and missed follow-up, so this is one of the most heavily tested practical skills. The trap is mirroring: students often assume 3 o'clock is lateral on both sides. Work it out each time by imagining yourself facing the patient. Another trap is measuring distance from the edge of the areola instead of the nipple. Exam items may give a lesion in the left upper outer quadrant and ask for the correct clock range, or give a clock time and ask whether it is medial or lateral.
on the registry: Expect items converting quadrants to clock positions for each breast and asking which elements a complete annotation must include.
checkpoint: Right 9 and left 3 are both lateral

title: Radial and Antiradial Scanning
front clue: Radial follows the duct like a spoke; antiradial crosses it at 90 degrees
core concept: Because the lobes and ducts radiate from the nipple like spokes of a wheel, ducts are best displayed with the transducer oriented along the radius toward the nipple (radial plane). The antiradial plane is perpendicular to the radial plane. Every lesion should be documented in two orthogonal planes, with and without calipers, using either radial and antiradial or transverse and sagittal views. The radial plane is best for showing ductal extension of carcinoma, intraductal masses, and duct ectasia, and for demonstrating the branch pattern of a malignancy. Survey scanning of the whole breast can be performed in overlapping rows (lawnmower pattern in transverse and sagittal) or in a radial pattern around the nipple. Measurements are taken in three dimensions: the longest dimension and its perpendicular in one plane, and the third dimension in the orthogonal plane. Overlap of each sweep is required so no tissue is skipped.
why it matters: Think of radial scanning as scanning the anatomy the way the breast is built. A mass that seems oval in an antiradial plane may reveal a tail extending toward the nipple in the radial plane, which is duct extension and raises suspicion. Orthogonal planes also distinguish a true mass (seen in both planes) from a fat lobule or tissue fold (which elongates or disappears in the second plane). A trap is documenting only one plane, which can hide orientation: a mass is not parallel whenever its long axis does not lie along the skin line (taller than wide, oblique, or round), and that judgment should hold up in both planes.
on the registry: Tested as which plane best shows ductal extension (radial) and the requirement to document lesions in two orthogonal planes.
checkpoint: Radial runs with the ducts; antiradial runs across them
ai_review_note: whyLock (high): BI-RADS defines not parallel as any long axis not oriented along the skin line: taller than wide, obliquely oriented, and round masses all qualify, so 'only if taller than wide' is wrong.

title: Transducer and Focal Zone Optimization
front clue: High-frequency linear probe, focus at the lesion, fat set to mid-gray
core concept: Breast imaging uses a high-frequency, broad-bandwidth linear array transducer; ACR and AIUM guidance calls for a center frequency of at least 10 MHz, and many systems operate at 12 to 18 MHz for superficial tissue. Higher frequency improves axial and lateral resolution at the cost of penetration, so a large breast or deep lesion may require a lower setting. Depth should include the pectoralis major so the full thickness of the breast is seen. The focal zone is placed at or just deep to the level of the lesion to narrow the beam and sharpen lateral resolution; multiple focal zones improve uniformity but lower frame rate. Overall gain and time gain compensation are adjusted so that subcutaneous fat appears medium gray and a simple cyst is truly anechoic; too much gain fills cysts with false echoes, too little makes solid masses look cystic. For very superficial lesions in the skin or just below it, a standoff pad or a thick layer of gel moves the lesion into the focal zone.
why it matters: Most cyst-versus-solid mistakes are knobology mistakes. If a cyst shows internal echoes, check that gain is not too high and the focus is at the cyst. If a hypoechoic solid mass looks anechoic, gain may be too low; Doppler and harmonics help. Exam items often describe an artifact and ask which control corrects it. A trap is setting the focus at the top of the image out of habit: focus belongs at the depth of interest. Another trap is choosing a curvilinear probe; lower frequency and wide sector geometry degrade near-field breast detail.
on the registry: Expect questions on transducer choice, where to place the focal zone, how to set gain using fat as a reference, and when to use a standoff pad.
checkpoint: Linear, high frequency, focus at the lesion, fat looks gray

title: Spatial Compounding and Harmonics
front clue: Compounding smooths speckle and margins but softens shadows and enhancement
core concept: Spatial compound imaging electronically steers the beam to acquire several frames from different angles and averages them into one image. Averaging reduces speckle, noise, and angle-dependent artifacts, improves the continuity of margins and specular reflectors such as Cooper ligaments and capsules, and makes tissue planes and needles easier to see. Because each part of the image is insonated from multiple directions, compounding also reduces posterior acoustic shadowing and posterior acoustic enhancement, which are useful diagnostic signs; turning compounding off can restore them when characterization depends on posterior features. Compounding may slightly reduce frame rate and can blur fast motion. Tissue harmonic imaging forms the image from harmonic frequencies generated in tissue at twice the transmitted frequency; it reduces clutter and reverberation, improves contrast resolution and lateral resolution, and helps clear artifactual echoes from cysts and improve conspicuity of hypoechoic masses and margins. Its trade-off is reduced penetration. Speckle reduction filters are post-processing tools with similar smoothing effects.
why it matters: The key reasoning is that every tool trades something away. Compounding gives prettier margins but can hide the shadow that makes a cancer suspicious or the enhancement that confirms a cyst. If an exam item asks why a mass appeared to lose its posterior shadowing on a newer system, compounding is the likely answer. Harmonics is the go-to answer for clearing reverberation and clutter inside a cyst. A trap is thinking compounding increases shadowing; it reduces it.
on the registry: Tested as the effect of compounding on posterior features and speckle, and the benefit of harmonics for cyst clutter and contrast.
checkpoint: Compounding cuts speckle and shadows; harmonics cut clutter

title: Breast Elastography
front clue: Cancers tend to be stiff, and look bigger on the elastogram than in gray scale
core concept: Elastography assesses tissue stiffness, which adds information to gray-scale features. Strain elastography uses gentle manual compression or physiologic motion and displays relative deformation: soft tissue deforms more, stiff tissue less. It is qualitative or semiquantitative, using a color map, a 5-point elasticity score (Tsukuba), or a strain ratio comparing the lesion with nearby fat. Shear wave elastography uses an acoustic radiation force push to generate shear waves and measures their speed, displayed in meters per second or converted to kilopascals; stiffer tissue has faster shear waves. It is quantitative and less operator dependent, but excessive preload pressure falsely raises stiffness, so minimal compression is required. Malignant masses are generally stiffer than benign ones, and a lesion that measures larger on the strain elastogram than on gray scale suggests malignancy. Some strain systems show a bull's-eye artifact in simple cysts. BI-RADS includes elasticity as an associated feature: soft, intermediate, or hard.
why it matters: Elastography is a supplement, not a replacement: it may help downgrade a low-suspicion oval mass or support biopsy of an equivocal one, but it does not override suspicious B-mode features. Pitfalls are worth memorizing. Some cancers are soft (mucinous, necrotic, or high-grade circumscribed tumors), and some benign lesions are stiff (fat necrosis, calcified fibroadenoma, sclerotic scars). Deep lesions and very small lesions yield unreliable results. Too much probe pressure is the most common user error in shear wave imaging. Exam items often ask which technique is quantitative (shear wave) or which finding favors malignancy.
on the registry: Expect questions comparing strain and shear wave methods, units of measurement, the effect of preload, and which elastographic findings suggest malignancy.
checkpoint: Strain is relative; shear wave is measured; stiff and bigger is worrisome

title: Breast Doppler Settings
front clue: Low PRF, low filter, light touch: breast vessels are small and slow
core concept: Breast vessels are small and carry slow flow, so Doppler must be set for sensitivity. Use power Doppler or a color mode with low pulse repetition frequency (low velocity scale), a low wall filter, and color gain increased until noise just appears and then slightly reduced. Keep the color box small and just larger than the lesion to maintain frame rate. Apply minimal transducer pressure, because compression easily obliterates flow in small vessels. BI-RADS describes vascularity as absent, internal, or vessels in the rim. Internal vascularity proves a mass is solid and excludes a simple or complicated cyst, which is especially helpful for hypoechoic masses that mimic cysts. Penetrating, disorganized, or branching internal vessels are associated with malignancy, while peripheral rim flow is common around inflamed cysts, abscesses, and benign masses. Twinkling artifact behind calcifications or biopsy clips can help locate them. Absence of flow does not exclude malignancy, since many small cancers show little detectable flow.
why it matters: The practical lesson is that the default settings are often wrong for the breast. If an obviously solid mass shows no flow, lower the scale and the filter and lighten your pressure before concluding it is avascular. Exam items commonly ask which change increases sensitivity to slow flow, or what Doppler finding distinguishes a solid hypoechoic mass from a complicated cyst. A trap is equating avascular with benign; another is mistaking motion or flash artifact for flow. Vascularity is supportive, not diagnostic, and must be interpreted with gray-scale features.
on the registry: Tested as the settings that improve detection of slow flow and the role of internal vascularity in confirming a solid mass.
checkpoint: Slow flow needs low scale, low filter, and almost no pressure

title: Simple Cyst
front clue: Anechoic, round or oval, thin wall, bright behind: benign and done
core concept: A simple cyst is the most common breast mass, typically in women aged 35 to 50, and arises from fluid accumulation in the TDLU. Strict sonographic criteria are: anechoic contents, circumscribed margin, oval or round shape, an imperceptible or thin echogenic wall, and posterior acoustic enhancement. Thin edge (refractive) shadowing at the lateral margins is common and acceptable. When all criteria are met the cyst is BI-RADS 2 (benign), and no follow-up or aspiration is needed unless it is painful or the patient requests relief. Cysts are often multiple and bilateral, and they fluctuate with the menstrual cycle and hormone therapy. They may be palpable, tender, and rapidly appearing. Very small cysts can show artifactual internal echoes from slice thickness or reverberation; harmonics, compounding, focal zone adjustment, and correct gain help clear them. A cyst should show no internal vascularity on Doppler.
why it matters: The simple cyst is the anchor for every cystic-lesion question: learn the five criteria and you can recognize when a lesion deviates from them. If one criterion fails, the lesion is no longer simple; it becomes complicated or complex, and management changes. A trap is calling a markedly hypoechoic solid mass a cyst because the gain is low; check for enhancement, increase gain, and use Doppler. Another trap is recommending follow-up for a simple cyst; it is benign and needs none. Ultrasound is the definitive test for confirming a cyst seen as a circumscribed mass on mammography.
on the registry: Expect recall of the sonographic criteria, the BI-RADS category (2), and items asking what management a simple cyst requires.
checkpoint: Anechoic, circumscribed, thin wall, enhancement equals BI-RADS 2

title: Complicated and Complex Cystic Masses
front clue: Debris alone is complicated; any solid part makes it complex and biopsy-worthy
core concept: A complicated cyst meets most simple cyst criteria but contains homogeneous low-level internal echoes, a fluid-debris level, or echoes that shift with position, without any solid component, thick wall, or internal vascularity. Contents may be proteinaceous fluid, blood, pus, or milk. Multiple bilateral complicated cysts are usually BI-RADS 2; a solitary complicated cyst is usually BI-RADS 3 with short-interval follow-up, or it may be aspirated. Clustered microcysts, a cluster of tiny anechoic foci each under 2 to 3 mm separated by thin (under 0.5 mm) septations, are typically BI-RADS 2 or 3. A complex cystic and solid mass contains both anechoic and echogenic solid elements: a thick wall, thick septations, an intracystic mass or mural nodule, or predominantly solid tissue with cystic spaces. Internal vascularity in the solid part confirms tissue. Complex cystic and solid masses are BI-RADS 4 and require biopsy, targeting the solid component. The differential includes intracystic papilloma, papillary carcinoma, necrotic invasive carcinoma, abscess, hematoma, and fat necrosis.
why it matters: Sort cystic lesions by asking one question: is there anything solid? If not, the lesion is either simple or complicated, both benign or probably benign. If yes, it is complex, and biopsy is indicated. Doppler and patient repositioning are your tools: moving debris and absent flow favor a complicated cyst, while a fixed nodule with flow means tissue. Common traps include labeling a cyst with fine septations or debris as complex, and forgetting that thick septations count as a solid component. Note that the BI-RADS 5th edition replaced the older term complex cyst with complex cystic and solid mass.
on the registry: Tested heavily: classify a described cystic lesion, give its BI-RADS category, and choose the next step (follow-up, aspiration, or biopsy).
checkpoint: Debris only: complicated; solid part: complex, biopsy it
ai_review_note: corePiece (high): BI-RADS defines clustered microcysts as a cluster of anechoic foci each smaller than 2 to 3 mm with thin (under 0.5 mm) intervening septations, not cysts under about 5 mm.

title: Fibroadenoma
front clue: Young woman, oval, parallel, circumscribed, gently lobulated, thin capsule
core concept: Fibroadenoma is the most common solid breast mass in women under 30 and the most common benign solid tumor overall. It is a fibroepithelial lesion of the TDLU containing stromal and epithelial elements, is estrogen sensitive, may enlarge in pregnancy or with hormone therapy, and involutes after menopause, often developing coarse popcorn calcifications. Clinically it is firm, rubbery, mobile, and painless. Classic sonographic features are an oval shape, parallel (wider than tall) orientation, circumscribed margins, a thin echogenic pseudocapsule, homogeneous hypoechoic or isoechoic echotexture, and two or three gentle macrolobulations; posterior features are often neutral or mildly enhancing, and calcified ones shadow. Internal flow may be present. A mass with these classic features is often assessed BI-RADS 3 with short-interval follow-up, while new or growing masses may be biopsied. Variants include the complex fibroadenoma (with cysts or calcifications) and the juvenile fibroadenoma in adolescents, which can grow rapidly beyond 5 cm. Phyllodes tumor is the key differential for a large, rapidly growing mass in women aged 40 to 50.
why it matters: Fibroadenoma is the benign template for the solid mass: it has none of the suspicious features. Reason by elimination: if any spiculation, angular margin, nonparallel orientation, microlobulation, or shadowing appears, the lesion no longer fits and should be biopsied. A trap is assuming a circumscribed mass in an older woman is a fibroadenoma, because circumscribed carcinomas such as mucinous and triple-negative cancers mimic it. Another is missing a phyllodes tumor, which looks like a fibroadenoma but is larger, grows faster, and may contain cystic clefts.
on the registry: Expect items naming the most common solid mass in young women, its classic features, popcorn calcifications in older patients, and phyllodes tumor as the differential.
checkpoint: Under 30, oval, parallel, circumscribed: think fibroadenoma

title: Fibrocystic Change
front clue: Cyclic, bilateral, tender lumps that wax and wane with the menstrual cycle
core concept: Fibrocystic change is the most common benign breast condition, affecting women aged about 30 to 50; it is called a change rather than a disease because it is a response to cyclic hormonal stimulation. Symptoms are bilateral breast pain, tenderness, and lumpiness that worsen in the luteal phase before menses, often most prominent in the upper outer quadrants. Histologic components include cysts (micro and macro), stromal fibrosis, apocrine metaplasia, ductal ectasia, and adenosis. On ultrasound the breast shows dense, echogenic fibroglandular tissue with scattered simple, complicated, or clustered microcysts, sometimes with mildly dilated ducts. Fibrosis can produce focal areas of shadowing that may mimic carcinoma. Sclerosing adenosis, a proliferative variant, can appear as an irregular mass or distortion with calcifications and often requires biopsy. Most fibrocystic change carries no increased cancer risk; proliferative lesions with atypia, such as atypical ductal hyperplasia, do raise risk. Symptoms usually subside after menopause unless hormone therapy is used.
why it matters: Fibrocystic change is a diagnosis of pattern, not of a single mass. When a patient describes bilateral cyclic pain, expect cysts and dense tissue; do not let a dominant suspicious mass hide among them. A focal shadowing area without cysts should be treated as a possible lesion, not dismissed as fibrosis. A trap is assuming fibrocystic change means high cancer risk; nonproliferative change does not. Exam items often describe the symptom pattern and timing and ask for the most likely diagnosis.
on the registry: Tested with a scenario of cyclic bilateral pain in a premenopausal woman and questions about which components are present and which raise risk.
checkpoint: Fibrocystic: cyclic, bilateral, cysts plus fibrosis

title: Intraductal Papilloma
front clue: Spontaneous bloody single-duct discharge: look for a mass inside a dilated duct
core concept: Intraductal papilloma is a benign proliferation of ductal epithelium on a fibrovascular core, and it is the most common cause of spontaneous, unilateral, single-duct bloody or serous nipple discharge. Central (solitary) papillomas arise in the large subareolar ducts, usually in women aged 30 to 50, and present with discharge. Peripheral (multiple) papillomas arise in the TDLUs, are often clinically silent, and are associated with a higher risk of atypia and carcinoma. On ultrasound a papilloma appears as an oval, circumscribed, hypoechoic or isoechoic solid mass within a dilated duct, as an intracystic mass, or as a solid mass that fills the duct. Power Doppler often shows a vascular stalk entering the mass, which separates it from debris. Scanning in the radial plane with minimal compression, and with the probe at the areolar edge, best shows the duct and its contents. Galactography (ductography) shows a filling defect or duct cutoff. Because papillary carcinoma can look identical, most papillomas are biopsied (BI-RADS 4), often with vacuum assistance.
why it matters: Pathologic nipple discharge is spontaneous, unilateral, from a single duct, and bloody or clear; physiologic discharge is bilateral, multiductal, and expressed. When the history is pathologic, scan radially in the subareolar region with light pressure, since heavy compression empties the duct and hides the lesion. A trap is assuming bloody discharge means cancer; papilloma is far more common, though cancer must be excluded. Another trap is mistaking inspissated debris for a papilloma; debris moves and has no flow.
on the registry: Expect a scenario of spontaneous bloody nipple discharge asking for the most likely cause and the best scanning technique to find it.
checkpoint: Bloody single-duct discharge: papilloma until proven otherwise

title: Mastitis, Abscess and Galactocele
front clue: Nursing mother: red painful breast is mastitis; a pocket of pus or milk changes management
core concept: Mastitis is inflammation of the breast, most often lactational and caused by Staphylococcus aureus entering through cracked nipples in the first weeks postpartum. Nonlactational (periductal) mastitis occurs in the subareolar region, especially in smokers. Ultrasound shows skin thickening, increased echogenicity of edematous fat, blurred tissue planes, and hyperemia, and its role is to look for abscess. An abscess appears as a hypoechoic or complex fluid collection with irregular or thick echogenic walls, internal debris or septations, posterior enhancement, peripheral hyperemia, and no internal flow; it is treated with antibiotics plus ultrasound-guided aspiration or drainage. A galactocele is a milk-filled retention cyst that develops during lactation or after weaning and is the most common benign mass in lactating women. Its appearance varies with milk composition: anechoic, complex with low-level echoes, or showing a fat-fluid level with echogenic fat layering on top. Older galactoceles become more echogenic and can mimic solid masses.
why it matters: Ultrasound earns its place here by answering one practical question: is there a drainable collection? If mastitis fails to improve within about 48 to 72 hours of appropriate antibiotics, scan for abscess; if findings persist after 1 to 2 weeks of treatment without a collection, especially when the patient is not lactating or has no fever, consider inflammatory carcinoma, the dangerous mimic. The fat-fluid level is the clue that a lactation-related mass is a galactocele. A trap is assuming internal echoes always mean infection; milk can be echogenic. Another is forgetting that core biopsy in a lactating breast carries a small risk of milk fistula.
on the registry: Tested with postpartum scenarios: identify mastitis versus abscess, recognize a fat-fluid level as a galactocele, and know when to suspect inflammatory cancer.
checkpoint: Lactation plus fat-fluid level is a galactocele
ai_review_status: fixed by AI review - please confirm
ai_review_note: whyLock (medium): Lactational mastitis guidance (e.g., Academy of Breastfeeding Medicine) calls for ultrasound to look for abscess when there is no improvement within about 48 to 72 hours of appropriate antibiotics; waiting one to two weeks delays abscess detection. Persistence beyond about 1 to 2 weeks is the trigger to consider inflammatory carcinoma.

title: Fat Necrosis and Lipoma
front clue: History of trauma or surgery: fat that has died can look like anything
core concept: Fat necrosis is a benign inflammatory reaction to injury of fat, caused by blunt trauma, surgery (lumpectomy, reduction, reconstruction), radiation, or biopsy; many patients do not recall the injury. It usually lies in the subcutaneous fat near the scar or trauma site. The sonographic appearance evolves over time: early, increased echogenicity of the fat with edema; then an oil cyst, an anechoic or complex cyst that may show a fat-fluid level and later an echogenic calcified rim (eggshell calcification); and late, an irregular hypoechoic mass with shadowing that can mimic carcinoma. Mammography showing a lucent, fat-containing oil cyst is diagnostic and avoids biopsy. A lipoma is a benign encapsulated tumor of mature fat, usually in the subcutaneous zone. On ultrasound it is oval, parallel, circumscribed, isoechoic to fat or slightly hyperechoic, with thin echogenic septations, is soft and compressible, and has little or no flow. A classic lipoma is BI-RADS 2.
why it matters: Both lesions are about fat, so compare them with the surrounding fat. A lipoma looks like a well-defined island of fat that compresses easily. Fat necrosis looks variable, and history is the best clue: always ask about trauma or surgery at that site. The trap is that late fat necrosis can be irregular, shadowing, stiff on elastography, and even spiculated on mammography, so it can mimic carcinoma; when imaging is not diagnostic, biopsy is still appropriate. Another trap is calling a lipoma a hypoechoic mass when it is simply isoechoic to fat.
on the registry: Expect scenarios with prior surgery or trauma asking for the likely diagnosis, and items describing a soft, compressible, fat-isoechoic mass.
checkpoint: Fat necrosis is the great mimic; lipoma is just organized fat

title: Gynecomastia
front clue: Male lump directly behind the nipple: think gynecomastia; eccentric and irregular: think cancer
core concept: Gynecomastia is benign proliferation of glandular and stromal tissue in the male breast caused by an increased estrogen to androgen ratio. It has a trimodal age distribution: neonates (maternal hormones), puberty, and older men. Causes include medications (spironolactone, anabolic steroids, antiandrogens, digoxin, some antidepressants), cirrhosis, hyperthyroidism, renal failure, testicular tumors, Klinefelter syndrome, and marijuana use. It can be unilateral or bilateral and is often tender. Ultrasound shows retroareolar tissue centered on the nipple in three patterns: nodular (early or florid), a fan-shaped or disc-shaped hypoechoic region; dendritic (chronic or fibrotic), a hypoechoic center with branching, finger-like projections into surrounding fat; and diffuse glandular, resembling a heterogeneously dense female breast, typically with estrogen therapy. Pseudogynecomastia is fat deposition without glandular tissue. Male breast cancer accounts for about 1 percent of breast cancers and appears as an irregular, hypoechoic mass usually eccentric to the nipple, sometimes with nipple retraction or bloody discharge.
why it matters: In a male patient, location relative to the nipple is your first discriminator. Gynecomastia is centered behind the nipple; cancer is usually eccentric and behaves like a female breast cancer with irregular margins and shadowing. Always obtain the medication and medical history, since drug-induced gynecomastia is common and reversible. The dendritic pattern's spiky projections can look alarming but are symmetric around the nipple. A trap is biopsying physiologic pubertal gynecomastia, which usually resolves on its own; another is forgetting that testicular tumors can cause it, so a scrotal ultrasound may be indicated.
on the registry: Tested as the most common male breast condition, its three sonographic patterns, common drug causes, and features that distinguish male breast cancer.
checkpoint: Centered on the nipple: gynecomastia; off center: worry

title: Suspicious Sonographic Features
front clue: Taller than wide, spiculated, angular, shadowing: one bad feature outweighs many good ones
core concept: Malignant masses tend to grow across tissue planes and provoke a desmoplastic reaction, which creates a recognizable set of features. Shape: irregular. Orientation: not parallel, meaning taller than wide, with the long axis crossing tissue planes. Margins: not circumscribed, described as indistinct, angular, microlobulated, or spiculated; spiculation is the most predictive. An echogenic halo (a thick, ill-defined bright rim) often accompanies infiltrative margins. Posterior features: shadowing, from desmoplasia, although high-grade tumors may show enhancement. Echo pattern: usually hypoechoic or heterogeneous. Associated features include microcalcifications within the mass, duct extension and branch pattern toward or away from the nipple, architectural distortion, disruption of Cooper ligaments, skin thickening or retraction, and internal penetrating vascularity, with hard stiffness on elastography. The classic teaching, drawn from early sonographic research, is that the presence of any single suspicious feature excludes a probably benign assessment, whereas a benign call requires absence of all suspicious features.
why it matters: The safest reasoning on the exam is asymmetric: suspicious features dominate. A mass that is oval and parallel but has a short angular margin is suspicious, not benign. When a question lists several features and asks which is most predictive of malignancy, spiculation and nonparallel orientation are strong choices. A trap is relying on posterior shadowing alone; fibrosis, fat necrosis, scars, and calcified fibroadenomas also shadow, and some cancers enhance. Another trap is treating marked hypoechogenicity alone as diagnostic. Report each feature with BI-RADS terms.
on the registry: Expect items asking which feature is most suspicious, which features exclude BI-RADS 3, and which described mass most warrants biopsy.
checkpoint: Any one suspicious feature beats all the benign ones

title: Invasive Ductal Carcinoma
front clue: The most common breast cancer: irregular, hypoechoic, spiculated, shadowing
core concept: Invasive ductal carcinoma, now termed invasive carcinoma of no special type (NST), accounts for about 70 to 80 percent of invasive breast cancers. It arises in the TDLU and breaches the basement membrane to invade surrounding stroma, provoking a desmoplastic fibrous reaction. Clinically it presents as a hard, fixed, painless lump, sometimes with skin dimpling, nipple retraction, or axillary adenopathy, or is found on screening. The classic sonographic appearance is an irregular, hypoechoic, nonparallel (taller than wide) mass with spiculated or angular margins, an echogenic halo, and posterior acoustic shadowing. Microcalcifications, duct extension, architectural distortion, Cooper ligament disruption, and internal penetrating vessels are frequent associated findings. High-grade tumors grow quickly and may instead appear more circumscribed and round with posterior enhancement, mimicking benign masses. Prognosis depends on size, nodal status, grade, and receptor status (estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, and HER2). Most are BI-RADS 4C or 5 and are confirmed by ultrasound-guided core biopsy.
why it matters: IDC is the default answer when an exam item describes a classic suspicious mass in a woman over 40 and asks for the most likely diagnosis. Once you identify it, think about extent: scan for satellite lesions, multifocal or multicentric disease, duct extension, and the axilla. A trap is the high-grade or triple-negative tumor that looks circumscribed; age, rapid growth, and subtle margin irregularity give it away. Another trap is underestimating size: the echogenic halo is part of the tumor and should be included when measuring.
on the registry: Tested as the most common breast cancer and its classic appearance, and as the mass to measure, including the echogenic halo.
checkpoint: IDC: most common, irregular, shadowing; include the halo

title: Invasive Lobular Carcinoma
front clue: Single-file cells, no discrete mass: subtle shadowing that is easy to miss
core concept: Invasive lobular carcinoma is the second most common invasive breast cancer, about 10 to 15 percent of cases. Its cells have lost the adhesion molecule E-cadherin, so they infiltrate stroma in single-file lines without forming a cohesive mass or provoking much desmoplasia. As a result, ILC is often clinically subtle (thickening rather than a lump) and difficult to detect on mammography and ultrasound. Sonographic appearances include an ill-defined hypoechoic area, an irregular mass with angular or indistinct margins, architectural distortion, or a region of posterior acoustic shadowing without a discrete mass. ILC is more often multifocal, multicentric, and bilateral than IDC, and imaging tends to underestimate its size. Breast MRI is the preferred modality for evaluating extent in many practices. It metastasizes to unusual sites such as the peritoneum, gastrointestinal tract, ovaries, and meninges. Lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS), now viewed mainly as a risk marker, is usually an incidental biopsy finding without a sonographic signature.
why it matters: The lesson from ILC is to trust a subtle finding. If an area of shadowing persists in both planes and with compression and does not behave like a ligament artifact, it may be lobular carcinoma rather than fibrosis. A trap is assuming that a negative mammogram excludes cancer in a palpable thickening; ILC is a classic false negative. Another trap is measuring only the visible portion; ILC is frequently larger than it appears. Exam items often ask which cancer is most associated with bilateral or multicentric disease or which tumor lacks E-cadherin.
on the registry: Expect items on E-cadherin loss, single-file growth, subtle shadowing without a mass, and the tendency toward multicentric and bilateral disease.
checkpoint: Lobular: single file, subtle shadow, often more than one site

title: Ductal Carcinoma In Situ
front clue: Cancer still inside the duct: found by calcifications on mammography more than by ultrasound
core concept: Ductal carcinoma in situ is a malignant proliferation of ductal epithelium confined within the basement membrane; it has not invaded stroma and is therefore stage 0 (Tis). It is graded low, intermediate, or high, and high-grade (comedo) DCIS contains central necrosis that calcifies. Most DCIS is detected on screening mammography as microcalcifications, especially fine linear or fine linear branching calcifications in a linear or segmental distribution, or as fine pleomorphic clusters. Ultrasound is less sensitive but can show echogenic microcalcifications within a hypoechoic mass or area, dilated ducts filled with echogenic material, an intraductal mass, or a nonmass hypoechoic region; high-frequency transducers and compounding improve detection of calcifications. When calcifications are the only finding, stereotactic (mammography-guided) vacuum-assisted biopsy is usual. Untreated DCIS can progress to invasive carcinoma, and invasion may already be present at surgery, so a biopsy diagnosis of DCIS can be upgraded. Paget disease of the nipple is frequently associated with underlying DCIS or invasive cancer.
why it matters: The key concept is the basement membrane: inside it is in situ, through it is invasive. That one line explains why DCIS is stage 0 and why it rarely spreads to nodes. On the exam, the modality question is common: mammography finds DCIS by its calcifications, and ultrasound plays a supporting role, mainly to find an associated mass that might represent invasion and to guide biopsy of it. A trap is believing a normal breast ultrasound excludes DCIS; it does not. Another is confusing DCIS with LCIS, which is primarily a risk marker.
on the registry: Tested as stage 0 disease, its classic mammographic calcification pattern, and the limited but useful role of ultrasound.
checkpoint: DCIS: inside the membrane, stage 0, seen as calcifications

title: Inflammatory Breast Cancer
front clue: Red, swollen, orange-peel breast without fever or response to antibiotics
core concept: Inflammatory breast cancer is an aggressive form accounting for about 1 to 5 percent of breast cancers. It is a clinical diagnosis: rapid onset, within about 6 months, of erythema and edema involving at least one third of the breast, often with warmth, enlargement, and peau d'orange (orange-peel skin). The skin changes are caused by tumor emboli blocking dermal lymphatics, not by infection. It is staged T4d, at least stage IIIB. Ultrasound findings include marked skin thickening (well over the normal 2 to 3 mm), increased echogenicity and edema of subcutaneous fat, dilated dermal and subcutaneous lymphatics seen as anechoic branching channels, and sometimes an underlying irregular mass or diffuse infiltrative change. Abnormal axillary nodes are common. Diagnosis is confirmed by core biopsy of any mass and skin punch biopsy. Unlike mastitis, it usually occurs in nonlactating women without fever or leukocytosis and does not respond to antibiotics.
why it matters: The essential skill is separating this disease from mastitis, because the treatments are opposite and delay is dangerous. In a scenario of a red, swollen breast, look for clues: not breastfeeding, no fever, failure to improve with antibiotics, and peau d'orange favor carcinoma. Ultrasound shows edema in both conditions, so the presence of a drainable abscess favors infection, while an underlying mass or abnormal nodes favor cancer. A trap is answering abscess drainage when the scenario has already described failed antibiotic therapy without a collection.
on the registry: Expect a red, swollen breast scenario asking whether it is mastitis or inflammatory carcinoma, and recall of peau d'orange, dermal lymphatic emboli, and T4d.
checkpoint: Red breast, no fever, no response to antibiotics: think inflammatory cancer

title: Circumscribed Carcinomas
front clue: Not every cancer is spiculated: some round, enhancing masses are malignant
core concept: Several cancers can appear oval or round with circumscribed or microlobulated margins and posterior enhancement, mimicking a fibroadenoma or complicated cyst. Mucinous (colloid) carcinoma occurs mainly in older, often postmenopausal women; pure tumors are composed largely of extracellular mucin, appear isoechoic to fat or mildly hypoechoic, are often soft, show posterior enhancement, and carry a favorable prognosis. Medullary-type carcinoma, now grouped by the World Health Organization with invasive carcinoma of no special type showing medullary features, occurs in younger women, is linked to BRCA1 mutation, is often triple negative, and appears as a round, very hypoechoic, circumscribed or microlobulated mass with posterior enhancement. High-grade triple-negative carcinomas generally grow rapidly and can look deceptively benign. Papillary carcinoma may be a complex cystic and solid mass. Metastases to the breast (melanoma, lymphoma, lung) and lymphoma are usually round and circumscribed. Close inspection often reveals a short microlobulated or indistinct segment of margin, or a nonparallel axis.
why it matters: Use this card to break the habit of equating circumscribed with benign. In an older woman, a new oval mass is not a fibroadenoma until proven otherwise, because new fibroadenomas after menopause are uncommon. In a young BRCA carrier, a round very hypoechoic mass with enhancement deserves biopsy. Look hard at the margin: a single microlobulated segment makes it suspicious. Soft elastography readings do not reassure you with mucinous carcinoma. A trap is calling a mucinous carcinoma a complicated cyst; Doppler flow and a lack of cyst criteria point to solid tissue.
on the registry: Tested with scenarios of a circumscribed, enhancing mass in an older woman or a young BRCA carrier, asking for the likely diagnosis or next step.
checkpoint: Circumscribed and enhancing can still be cancer: check age and every margin

title: Staging Basics
front clue: TNM: tumor size in 2 cm steps, nodes, and distant metastasis
core concept: Breast cancer is staged with the AJCC TNM system; the 8th edition adds grade and receptor status to anatomic staging for prognostic stage groups. T describes the primary tumor by its greatest invasive dimension: Tis is in situ disease (DCIS); T1 is 2 cm or less (T1mi up to 1 mm, T1a over 1 to 5 mm, T1b over 5 to 10 mm, T1c over 10 to 20 mm); T2 is over 2 cm up to 5 cm; T3 is over 5 cm; T4 is any size with direct extension to the chest wall (not pectoralis alone) or skin (ulceration, satellite skin nodules, or peau d'orange), and T4d is inflammatory carcinoma. N describes regional nodes (axillary, internal mammary, supraclavicular), and M describes distant metastasis to sites such as bone, lung, liver, and brain. Ultrasound contributes by measuring the tumor in three dimensions, finding additional foci, and assessing nodes. Multifocal disease means more than one tumor in the same quadrant; multicentric means tumors in different quadrants, which may change surgical planning.
why it matters: The exam does not expect oncologist-level staging, but it does expect the 2 cm and 5 cm thresholds, what Tis and T4d mean, and the distinction between multifocal and multicentric. Accurate measurement is the sonographer's contribution: measure the longest dimension, including the echogenic halo, and report all three dimensions. A trap is assuming pectoralis invasion makes a tumor T4; chest wall means ribs, intercostal muscles, or serratus anterior. Another trap is overlooking a second lesion, which can shift the plan from lumpectomy to mastectomy.
on the registry: Expect questions converting a measured size to a T category and defining multifocal versus multicentric disease.
checkpoint: T1 up to 2, T2 up to 5, T3 over 5, T4 skin or chest wall

title: BI-RADS Mass Descriptors
front clue: Shape, orientation, margin, echo pattern, posterior features: five words describe any mass
core concept: The ACR BI-RADS ultrasound lexicon (5th edition, 2013) standardizes how masses are described. A mass is a space-occupying lesion seen in two planes. Shape: oval (including two or three gentle undulations), round, or irregular; the older term lobular was removed. Orientation: parallel (long axis parallel to the skin) or not parallel (taller than wide, including round). Margin: circumscribed, or not circumscribed, subdivided into indistinct, angular, microlobulated, and spiculated. Echo pattern relative to subcutaneous fat: anechoic, hyperechoic, complex cystic and solid, hypoechoic, isoechoic, or heterogeneous. Posterior features: no posterior features, enhancement, shadowing, or combined pattern. Background echotexture (tissue composition) is reported as homogeneous fat, homogeneous fibroglandular, or heterogeneous. Calcifications are described as in a mass, outside a mass, or intraductal. The echogenic rim previously called a halo is not a separate lexicon term but is described within margin assessment.
why it matters: The lexicon is the language of the exam. Learn each category with its exact allowable terms, because distractors often use near-miss words such as lobulated, ill-defined, or smooth that are not lexicon descriptors. Echogenicity is always relative to subcutaneous fat, not to glandular tissue: a mass equal to fat is isoechoic, and hyperechoic means brighter than fat or equal to fibroglandular tissue. A trap is calling a round mass parallel; round masses are classified as not parallel. Another is forgetting that one non-circumscribed descriptor makes the margin not circumscribed.
on the registry: Expect items asking which term is or is not in the lexicon, what echogenicity is referenced to, and how to classify a described mass.
checkpoint: Echogenicity is compared with fat; lobular is no longer a shape
ai_review_note: whyLock (high): BI-RADS 5th edition defines hyperechoic as increased echogenicity relative to fat or equal to fibroglandular tissue; it does not require the mass to be brighter than fibroglandular tissue.

title: Associated Features and Special Cases
front clue: Beyond the mass: distortion, ducts, skin, edema, flow, stiffness, and named special cases
core concept: BI-RADS associated features describe the tissue around or related to a finding: architectural distortion; duct changes (abnormal caliber or arborization, duct extension); skin changes (skin thickening, focal or diffuse over 2 mm, and skin retraction); edema; vascularity (absent, internal, or vessels in rim); and elasticity assessment (soft, intermediate, or hard). Special cases are findings with a unique diagnosis or appearance: simple cyst; clustered microcysts; complicated cyst; mass in or on skin (sebaceous or epidermal inclusion cyst, keloid, mole, neurofibroma, accessory nipple); foreign body including implants, clips, wires, catheter sleeves, and injected silicone or paraffin; intramammary and axillary lymph nodes; vascular abnormalities, including arteriovenous malformations and Mondor disease (superficial thrombophlebitis seen as a tubular, noncompressible, avascular vein); postsurgical fluid collection; and fat necrosis. Mondor disease presents as a painful cord, often after surgery or trauma, and is benign and self-limited.
why it matters: Associated features often decide the category when the mass itself is borderline. Skin thickening plus edema shifts thinking toward inflammatory processes or cancer; vessels in the rim favor a benign or inflammatory process, while internal penetrating flow favors solid tissue. Special cases are useful shortcuts: once a finding fits one, the management is usually clear, such as a mass in the skin, which is almost always benign. A trap is assuming a tender palpable cord is a cancer; Mondor disease is a noncompressible thrombosed vein. Another is forgetting that implants and clips are classified as foreign bodies.
on the registry: Tested as which findings are associated features versus special cases, and as recognition of Mondor disease and skin lesions.
checkpoint: Special cases come with their own answer; associated features shift the odds

title: BI-RADS Assessment Categories
front clue: Zero to six: each category comes with its own management
core concept: BI-RADS final assessment categories link imaging to action. Category 0, incomplete: additional imaging or prior studies needed; used sparingly at ultrasound. Category 1, negative: nothing to describe. Category 2, benign: for example simple cysts, intramammary nodes, implants, stable surgical changes, lipomas; routine screening. Category 3, probably benign: likelihood of malignancy 2 percent or less; short-interval follow-up, typically ultrasound at 6 months, then at 12 and 24 months (some use 6, 12, 24, and 36 months); typical findings are a circumscribed oval parallel solid mass, a solitary complicated cyst, and clustered microcysts. Category 4, suspicious: tissue diagnosis recommended, subdivided into 4A (more than 2 to 10 percent), 4B (more than 10 to 50 percent), and 4C (more than 50 to less than 95 percent). Category 5, highly suggestive of malignancy: 95 percent or greater; biopsy. Category 6, known biopsy-proven malignancy before definitive therapy. Assessment and management recommendations should be concordant.
why it matters: Think of the categories as a ladder of probability with fixed management at each step. Exam items often give a lesion description and ask for the category, or give a category and ask the recommendation. Remember that category 3 is reserved for specific findings with established low risk and should not be used as a hedge for a suspicious mass. A trap is putting a known cancer awaiting surgery in category 5 rather than 6. Another is recommending biopsy for category 3; follow-up is the standard, although biopsy may be done in specific clinical circumstances.
on the registry: Heavily tested: matching findings to categories, malignancy probabilities for 3, 4A to 4C, and 5, and the correct follow-up interval for category 3.
checkpoint: 3 is 2 percent or less with 6-month follow-up; 5 is 95 percent or more

title: Mammographic Correlation
front clue: Same lesion? Match location, size, shape, depth, and surrounding tissue
core concept: Targeted ultrasound often follows a mammographic finding, and the sonographer must confirm that the ultrasound finding is the same lesion. Use the craniocaudal (CC) view to determine medial versus lateral position and the mediolateral oblique (MLO) or true lateral (90 degree mediolateral or lateromedial) view to determine superior versus inferior position, then convert that to a clock position and distance from the nipple. Compared with a true lateral view, lateral lesions project higher and medial lesions lower on the MLO, so the true lateral view is more accurate for height. Compare size, shape, margins, and depth, and note surrounding tissue (fat versus glandular). Mammographic breast density categories are a (almost entirely fatty), b (scattered fibroglandular densities), c (heterogeneously dense), and d (extremely dense); dense breasts lower mammographic sensitivity and may warrant supplemental screening ultrasound. Mammography best shows calcifications and architectural distortion, while ultrasound best distinguishes cyst from solid mass. For a palpable lump, women under 30 usually start with ultrasound; at 40 and older, diagnostic mammography plus ultrasound.
why it matters: Correlation errors lead to biopsy of the wrong lesion, so the exam emphasizes how to confirm a match. If a mammographic mass is 1 cm and in fat, a 3 cm ultrasound mass in glandular tissue is probably not the same lesion. Clip placement and a post-biopsy mammogram close the loop. A trap is assuming the MLO view gives true height; it is oblique. Another is expecting ultrasound to see every mammographic calcification; most calcifications without a mass are biopsied stereotactically.
on the registry: Expect questions on which mammographic view gives which location, density categories, the initial imaging choice for palpable lumps by age, and confirming correlation.
checkpoint: CC tells medial or lateral; true lateral tells up or down

title: MRI Correlation and Second-Look Ultrasound
front clue: MRI finds it, ultrasound looks again, and the clip proves the match
core concept: Contrast-enhanced breast MRI is the most sensitive imaging test for invasive breast cancer. Indications include screening women at high risk (lifetime risk of about 20 percent or more, BRCA carriers, prior chest radiation), evaluating extent of a known cancer, assessing response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy, problem solving, and evaluating silicone implant integrity without contrast. When MRI shows an enhancing finding not seen on prior imaging, a targeted (second-look) ultrasound is performed to find a correlate. Because MRI is done prone with the breast hanging and ultrasound supine, lesion location shifts, so use the clock position, depth, distance from nipple, and nearby landmarks such as cysts, nodes, or vessels. Masses are more likely than nonmass enhancement to have a sonographic correlate, and a larger mass is easier to find. If found, ultrasound-guided biopsy with clip placement follows, and post-biopsy MRI or mammography may confirm that the correct lesion was sampled. If no correlate is found, MRI-guided biopsy is performed rather than follow-up.
why it matters: Second-look ultrasound is a hunt with a moving target. Expect the lesion to be slightly displaced compared with its MRI position because of the change from prone to supine, and use landmarks to stay oriented. Exam items may ask what to do when no correlate is found: the answer is MRI-guided biopsy, not dismissal. A trap is assuming that any ultrasound finding near the location is the correlate; it must match size, shape, and depth. Another is forgetting that MRI evaluates silicone implant rupture without contrast.
on the registry: Tested as the next step after an MRI-detected lesion, positioning differences, and the action when ultrasound finds no correlate.
checkpoint: No ultrasound correlate means MRI-guided biopsy

title: Reporting and Follow-Up
front clue: A complete report: what, where, how big, compared with what, what it means, what next
core concept: A breast ultrasound report includes the indication (screening, palpable lump, mammographic or MRI finding, pain, discharge), the area scanned, tissue composition for screening examinations, and a description of each finding with lexicon terms. Location is given by side, clock position, distance from the nipple, and optionally depth. Size is recorded in three dimensions. Comparison with prior studies notes stability or change, and correlation with physical, mammographic, or MRI findings is stated. Each report ends with a final BI-RADS assessment and a concordant management recommendation: routine screening, short-interval follow-up, or tissue sampling. For category 3 lesions, stability over about 2 years supports downgrading to category 2; an increase of about 20 percent or more in the longest dimension within 6 months, or new suspicious features, prompts biopsy. Findings that need urgent action should be communicated directly to the referring provider and documented. The sonographer records a technical impression for the interpreting physician but does not give the patient a diagnosis.
why it matters: Good reports are reproducible: another sonographer should find the same lesion from your labels and measurements. Exam questions often ask which element is missing from a description, what follow-up timeline applies, or who communicates results. A trap is reporting a probably benign lesion without a follow-up plan, which makes the report nonconcordant. Another is the sonographer discussing likely diagnoses with the patient; that is outside the sonographer's scope. Stability is defined against prior images, so obtaining comparisons is part of the job.
on the registry: Expect items on required report elements, category 3 follow-up timing and the criteria for upgrading, and the communication of critical results.
checkpoint: Describe, locate, measure, compare, categorize, recommend
