ai_review_note: corePiece (medium): The commonly cited BI-RADS/ACR growth threshold prompting biopsy of a probably benign mass is an increase of about 20 percent or more in the longest dimension (diameter) within 6 months, not 20 percent in volume.

title: Normal Lymph Node
front clue: Kidney-shaped node: thin dark cortex wrapped around a bright fatty hilum
core concept: A normal lymph node is oval or reniform (kidney shaped) with a thin, uniform, hypoechoic cortex surrounding an echogenic fatty hilum, through which the artery and vein enter. The long axis is usually parallel to the skin, and the length to width ratio is typically greater than 2. A cortical thickness of 3 mm or less is the most widely taught normal threshold, though sources range from about 2 to 3 mm. On color or power Doppler, flow, when seen, enters centrally through the hilum and branches symmetrically. Normal axillary nodes vary widely in length and may be over 1 cm long because of fatty hilar replacement, so size alone is a weak criterion; cortical morphology matters more. Intramammary lymph nodes are common, typically under 1 cm, located in the upper outer quadrant or axillary tail within the breast, and are classified as BI-RADS 2 when they have a classic appearance. Fatty replacement of the hilum increases with age.
why it matters: The normal node is the template: once you know it, abnormal nodes are defined by departures from it. The most useful questions to ask are whether the cortex is thin and even and whether the hilum is preserved. A trap is calling a large but fatty node abnormal; a long node with a thin cortex and a big fatty hilum is benign. Another trap is mistaking an intramammary node for a breast mass; look for the echogenic hilum and the hilar vessel. Scanning the node in its long axis best shows the hilum.
on the registry: Expect recall of the normal node's appearance, the commonly cited cortical thickness threshold, hilar flow, and the intramammary node as a benign finding.
checkpoint: Thin even cortex, bright hilum, hilar flow: normal

title: Abnormal Lymph Node Features
front clue: Thick or bulging cortex, lost hilum, round shape, peripheral flow
core concept: Lymph node metastases first lodge in the cortex, so the earliest sign is cortical change. Suspicious features include diffuse cortical thickening over about 3 mm; focal or eccentric cortical bulging (more worrisome than uniform thickening); compression, displacement, or complete loss of the fatty hilum; a round shape with a length to width ratio under 2; markedly hypoechoic cortex; irregular or indistinct margins suggesting extracapsular extension; peripheral or nonhilar (transcapsular) blood flow; matted or clustered nodes; and microcalcifications. Reactive nodes from infection, inflammation, or recent ipsilateral vaccination often show smooth, uniform cortical thickening with preserved hilum and hilar flow. Other causes of abnormal nodes include lymphoma (often markedly hypoechoic and sometimes pseudocystic), leukemia, rheumatoid arthritis, sarcoidosis, silicone uptake from ruptured implants, and metastases from other primaries such as melanoma, lung, and ovary. Suspicious nodes are sampled with ultrasound-guided core biopsy or FNA, and a clip may be placed before neoadjuvant therapy.
why it matters: Rank the features by how much they point toward tumor: focal eccentric bulging and loss of the hilum are the strongest, and a uniformly thick cortex with preserved hilum is less specific. Always correlate with history, such as a recent vaccine in the same arm, mastitis, or a known primary. A trap is ignoring a small node with an eccentric bulge because it is not enlarged. Another is assuming a node full of echogenic snowstorm material is cancer; in a patient with silicone implants, it may be silicone.
on the registry: Tested as which features are most suspicious for metastasis, which suggest a reactive process, and how abnormal nodes are sampled.
checkpoint: Eccentric bulge or lost hilum means sample the node

title: Axillary Levels
front clue: The pectoralis minor divides the axilla into levels I, II, and III
core concept: Axillary nodes are divided into three surgical levels by their relationship to the pectoralis minor muscle. Level I nodes lie lateral and inferior to the lateral border of the pectoralis minor; they include the low axillary nodes and are the most commonly involved and most often contain the sentinel node. Level II nodes lie deep (posterior) to the pectoralis minor and include the interpectoral (Rotter) nodes between the pectoralis major and minor. Level III nodes lie medial and superior to the medial border of the pectoralis minor, in the infraclavicular region. Metastatic spread usually progresses in order from level I to II to III; skip metastases to higher levels without lower-level involvement are uncommon. Supraclavicular and internal mammary nodes are regional nodes outside the axillary levels and indicate more advanced nodal stage when involved. Sonographically, the pectoralis minor is identified as a hypoechoic muscle deep to the pectoralis major, and the axillary vessels serve as landmarks for levels II and III.
why it matters: The single anatomic rule to memorize is that the pectoralis minor is the reference. Lateral and below is I, behind is II, medial and above is III. On the exam, expect an item describing the position of a node relative to the muscle and asking for the level, or asking which level holds Rotter nodes. A trap is assuming Rotter nodes are level I because they are low; they are interpectoral and therefore level II. Scanning the axilla should follow the axillary vessels upward to evaluate higher levels when a suspicious level I node is found.
on the registry: Expect questions identifying the muscle that defines the levels, the location of each level, and the level of Rotter nodes.
checkpoint: Pectoralis minor: lateral is I, behind is II, medial is III

title: Breast Implant Types
front clue: Saline or silicone, single or double lumen, in front of or behind the muscle
core concept: Breast implants have an elastomer silicone shell filled with saline or silicone gel; double-lumen implants usually have an inner silicone lumen and an outer saline lumen. Shells may be smooth or textured. They are placed either subglandular (prepectoral, between the gland and pectoralis major) or subpectoral (retropectoral, behind the muscle). The body forms a fibrous capsule around every implant; tightening of this capsule causes capsular contracture with firmness, pain, and distortion. On ultrasound a normal implant is anechoic with a smooth echogenic shell; the shell and capsule may appear as a thin trilaminar echogenic line. Reverberation artifact is common in the anterior implant and should not be mistaken for contents. Radial folds, infoldings of the shell extending from the periphery inward and connected to it, are normal. A small amount of peri-implant fluid can be normal, but a large late seroma, especially more than a year after placement of a textured implant, raises concern for breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma (BIA-ALCL), which is evaluated by aspiration for CD30 testing.
why it matters: Implant questions begin with type and location, because the signs of rupture depend on them. Saline rupture is usually obvious clinically: the implant deflates as saline is absorbed. Silicone rupture is often silent and requires imaging. Radial folds are the normal finding most confused with rupture: a radial fold connects to the periphery, whereas a collapsed shell floats free inside the gel. A trap is reading anterior reverberation as internal echoes. Another is forgetting BIA-ALCL in a patient with a delayed seroma around a textured implant.
on the registry: Tested as the anatomy of implant placement, the meaning of the fibrous capsule, radial folds as a normal finding, and recognition of BIA-ALCL.
checkpoint: Radial folds touch the edge; a collapsed shell floats inside

title: Intracapsular Rupture
front clue: Stepladder sign: collapsed shell lines stacked inside the gel
core concept: Intracapsular rupture is a tear of the silicone implant shell with the gel still contained by the surrounding fibrous capsule. It is the most common form of silicone implant rupture, often asymptomatic, and frequently found on imaging. Because the gel remains within the capsule, mammography is usually insensitive. On ultrasound, the collapsed shell floats within the gel and appears as multiple discontinuous, parallel or nearly parallel echogenic lines stacked inside the implant, the stepladder sign. Low-level echoes within the normally anechoic gel may also be present. On MRI, which is the most sensitive and specific test for silicone implant integrity, the collapsed shell produces the linguine sign: multiple curvilinear low-signal lines floating in the gel. Small amounts of silicone escaping through the shell but staying within the capsule may cause the keyhole, teardrop, or noose sign, which indicates a more subtle or early intracapsular rupture. Saline implants do not show these signs because the saline is resorbed when the shell fails.
why it matters: The reasoning is all about where the silicone is. If the gel is still inside the fibrous capsule, the signs are inside the implant; if it escapes the capsule, the signs appear in the breast tissue. Exam items commonly describe stacked lines in the implant and ask for the name of the sign or the type of rupture. A trap is confusing the stepladder sign with radial folds, which are connected to the periphery and are normal. Another is calling reverberation artifact in the anterior implant a stepladder sign.
on the registry: Tested as the stepladder sign on ultrasound, the linguine sign on MRI, and the most common form of silicone rupture.
checkpoint: Stepladder on ultrasound, linguine on MRI: intracapsular

title: Extracapsular Rupture
front clue: Snowstorm: bright, noisy echoes with dirty shadowing outside the implant
core concept: Extracapsular rupture occurs when silicone gel escapes through both the implant shell and the surrounding fibrous capsule into the breast tissue. It is less common than intracapsular rupture and nearly always accompanies it. The free silicone causes a granulomatous reaction, forming silicone granulomas (siliconomas). On ultrasound, free silicone produces the snowstorm sign: a highly echogenic area with diffuse, echogenic noise and dirty posterior acoustic shadowing that obscures deeper structures, caused by the very slow speed of sound in silicone and its mixture with tissue. Larger collections of free silicone may appear as anechoic or hypoechoic masses surrounded by echogenic tissue. Silicone can migrate to axillary lymph nodes, which then show the snowstorm appearance. Mammography shows dense silicone outside the implant contour. MRI confirms silicone outside the capsule. Free silicone injection, used in the past for augmentation, produces the same snowstorm pattern diffusely. Prior ruptured implants can leave residual silicone even after replacement.
why it matters: Snowstorm equals silicone in tissue. If the finding is outside the implant and blocks deeper visualization, the gel has escaped the capsule. A trap is calling the snowstorm a calcified or shadowing carcinoma; the history of silicone implants or injections and the diffuse echogenic noise give it away. Another trap is assuming an axillary node with snowstorm echoes is metastatic; in an implant patient, silicone uptake is more likely. Exam items commonly ask for the sign of extracapsular rupture or how silicone reaches the axilla.
on the registry: Tested as the snowstorm sign, silicone granulomas, and silicone in axillary nodes.
checkpoint: Snowstorm outside the implant: silicone has escaped the capsule

title: Core and Vacuum-Assisted Biopsy
front clue: Needle parallel to the chest wall, document pre-fire and post-fire, check concordance
core concept: Ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy is the standard method for sampling suspicious breast masses and nodes. A spring-loaded (automated) device, commonly 14 gauge, obtains several cores, usually at least four or five for masses, with multiple passes through the lesion. Vacuum-assisted biopsy (VAB) uses larger needles, about 7 to 11 gauge, with suction that draws tissue into the aperture, allowing larger contiguous samples through one insertion; it is preferred for small lesions, intraductal and papillary lesions, and calcifications, and can remove small lesions entirely. The needle is inserted with a freehand technique, aligned with the long axis of the transducer and as parallel to the chest wall as possible, to keep the entire needle visible and avoid pneumothorax. Images document the needle before firing and after firing through the lesion. After biopsy, radiologic-pathologic concordance is assessed: concordant benign results return to follow-up, discordant results need repeat biopsy or excision, and high-risk lesions such as atypical ductal hyperplasia may require surgical excision.
why it matters: The needle path is the most tested practical point: shallow, parallel, and fully visible. Steep angles make the needle hard to see and risk the chest wall. Planning the approach also means accounting for the throw of the spring-loaded device so the tip does not pass into the pectoralis or an implant. A trap is accepting a benign pathology result for a BI-RADS 5 mass; that is discordant and needs repeat sampling. Another is thinking VAB is required for every mass; standard core biopsy suffices for most.
on the registry: Expect questions on needle approach, gauge differences between core and vacuum devices, documentation images, and radiologic-pathologic concordance.
checkpoint: Parallel needle, pre-fire and post-fire images, concordance last

title: Fine-Needle Aspiration
front clue: Thin needle, cells only: quick and gentle but tells you less than a core
core concept: Fine-needle aspiration (FNA) uses a thin needle, typically 20 to 25 gauge, moved back and forth through a lesion with or without suction to collect cells for cytologic analysis. It is fast, inexpensive, causes minimal trauma, and is useful for sampling suspicious axillary lymph nodes, drainage of cysts, and confirming recurrence. Smears may be prepared at the bedside or fluid placed in preservative, and on-site cytology assessment improves adequacy. Its main limitation is that cytology examines individual cells without tissue architecture, so FNA cannot reliably distinguish in situ from invasive carcinoma, and it is less suitable for receptor testing and for many benign diagnoses. Nondiagnostic or insufficient samples are more common than with core biopsy and depend on operator and cytopathologist experience. For these reasons core needle biopsy is preferred for most breast masses. The needle tip must be visualized throughout, and the same aseptic technique, labeling, and documentation standards apply as for any procedure.
why it matters: The trade-off is simple: FNA gives cells, core biopsy gives tissue. When a question asks which method cannot tell in situ from invasive disease, the answer is FNA. When a question asks for the least invasive way to sample an abnormal axillary node, FNA is reasonable, although many centers use core biopsy. A trap is assuming FNA is preferred for all breast masses because it is less invasive; core biopsy offers more reliable diagnosis and receptor status.
on the registry: Tested as the needle size, what FNA can and cannot show compared with core biopsy, and typical uses such as axillary nodes.
checkpoint: FNA gives cells, core gives architecture

title: Cyst Aspiration
front clue: Drain it, look at it, and make sure nothing is left behind
core concept: Ultrasound-guided cyst aspiration is performed to relieve a painful or tense simple cyst, to confirm that an indeterminate lesion (such as a solitary complicated cyst) is fluid, and to drain abscesses or galactoceles. A needle, commonly 18 to 22 gauge, is advanced under real-time guidance into the cyst, and fluid is withdrawn until the cyst collapses completely. Fluid is commonly yellow, green, or cloudy; nonbloody fluid from a benign-appearing cyst that resolves completely is usually discarded. Bloody fluid, a residual mass after aspiration, or a solid component seen during aspiration prompts cytology and core biopsy, often with clip placement. Purulent fluid is sent for culture and sensitivity. Documentation includes the cyst before aspiration, the needle within it, and the collapsed site afterward. Recurrence is common, and repeated recurrence of the same cyst may warrant further evaluation. Complications are uncommon and include hematoma, infection, and vasovagal reaction.
why it matters: The key reasoning point is what happens after the fluid is out. Complete resolution plus nonbloody fluid means benign and done; anything left behind means tissue, and tissue needs sampling. A trap is sending all cyst fluid for cytology; routine cytology of clear or yellow-green fluid is generally not useful. Another is ignoring a residual mass because the patient's pain resolved. Questions frequently ask which fluid characteristic or post-aspiration finding requires further workup.
on the registry: Expect questions about indications, which fluid should be sent for cytology or culture, and what to do with a residual mass.
checkpoint: Bloody fluid or residual mass means biopsy

title: Clip and Marker Placement
front clue: Mark the spot: the clip lets everyone find what was sampled
core concept: A biopsy marker (clip) is a small, usually titanium or stainless steel, radiopaque device deployed through the biopsy needle or a dedicated introducer at the biopsy site. Indications include marking a lesion that may become hard to see after biopsy (small lesions, lesions removed by vacuum biopsy), marking a cancer before neoadjuvant chemotherapy so its location remains known if the tumor shrinks, marking biopsied axillary nodes for targeted axillary surgery, and confirming correlation between ultrasound, mammography, and MRI findings. Some markers are embedded in a hydrogel or collagen plug that improves sonographic visibility for weeks. On ultrasound a clip appears as a small, bright linear echo, sometimes with posterior shadowing or twinkling artifact. A post-procedure two-view mammogram (craniocaudal and true lateral) confirms the clip's position relative to the biopsy site. Clip migration of 1 cm or more is commonly considered significant; the accordion effect, re-expansion of tissue after release of compression, is a common cause. Shapes vary so multiple clips can be distinguished.
why it matters: Clips close the correlation loop: if a clip placed under ultrasound sits in the mammographic lesion on the post-procedure mammogram, the right lesion was sampled. Exam items may ask why a clip is placed before chemotherapy or what view confirms its position. A trap is placing no clip in a small mass that the vacuum device removed completely; without a marker the surgeon cannot find the site. Another is ignoring migration; the report must describe the clip's distance from the target so localization can be adjusted.
on the registry: Tested as indications for marker placement, the post-procedure mammogram, migration and the accordion effect, and marking before neoadjuvant chemotherapy.
checkpoint: Clip before chemo, mammogram after placement

title: Preoperative Localization
front clue: Guide the surgeon to a lesion they cannot feel: wire or wireless seed
core concept: Nonpalpable lesions or biopsy clips must be localized before surgical excision. With wire localization, a needle containing a hooked wire is placed under ultrasound or mammographic guidance, usually the day of surgery, so that the wire tip lies within or just beyond the lesion, ideally within about 1 cm, and the hook anchors it in place; the external end is taped and covered. Ultrasound guidance allows a shorter, more direct path that often parallels the chest wall. Wireless localization devices, such as radioactive iodine-125 seeds, magnetic seeds, radar reflectors, and radiofrequency identification tags, are implanted in the lesion and detected intraoperatively with a handheld probe; they can be placed days or more before surgery, improving scheduling and patient comfort. Bracketing with two devices marks the margins of larger lesions or calcifications. A post-localization mammogram documents the device position, and specimen radiography or ultrasound after excision confirms that the lesion, clip, and device were removed.
why it matters: Localization is a team process, so communication and documentation dominate test items. The sonographer should report the distance from the device tip to the lesion and the skin entry site, because the surgeon plans the incision from them. Wire problems include migration, transection, and dislodgement before surgery, which is why wires are placed the same day and patients are told not to pull or bump them. A trap is assuming wireless seeds avoid radiation regulation; radioactive seeds require tracking and handling under radiation safety rules. Specimen imaging is the confirmation step.
on the registry: Expect questions on wire versus wireless options, documenting device position, specimen radiography, and wire complications.
checkpoint: Wire the same day; seeds can wait; specimen image confirms removal

title: Procedure Complications
front clue: Hematoma is common; pneumothorax is rare and preventable with a parallel approach
core concept: Image-guided breast procedures are safe, but complications must be anticipated and managed. Hematoma and bleeding are the most common complications, more likely with vacuum-assisted devices and in patients on anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy; manual compression for several minutes after the procedure, typically about 5 to 10 minutes or longer, and ice packs reduce them. Infection is uncommon and minimized by aseptic technique. Vasovagal reaction, with pallor, sweating, nausea, bradycardia, and fainting, is managed by stopping the procedure, laying the patient flat, and raising the legs. Pneumothorax is rare and is prevented by keeping the needle parallel to the chest wall, especially in thin patients and with deep or axillary lesions. Other complications include implant rupture during biopsy near an implant, milk fistula when biopsying a lactating breast, pain, bruising, and very rarely needle tract seeding. Lidocaine allergy is rare, and patients should be asked about allergies before the procedure. Post-procedure instructions cover signs of bleeding and infection.
why it matters: When a scenario describes a complication, match it to its cause and its fix. Expanding swelling after biopsy is hematoma: apply pressure. A patient who becomes pale and lightheaded is having a vasovagal reaction: lay flat and elevate legs. Shortness of breath or chest pain after a deep axillary biopsy suggests pneumothorax and needs urgent evaluation. A trap is attributing post-procedure fainting to lidocaine toxicity; vasovagal reaction is far more common. Displacing an implant away from the needle path, a technique similar to implant displacement mammography, reduces rupture risk.
on the registry: Tested as the most common complication, prevention of pneumothorax, management of vasovagal reaction, and lactation-specific risks.
checkpoint: Bleeding is common, pneumothorax is rare, fainting is vasovagal

title: Informed Consent and Communication
front clue: Explain risks, benefits, alternatives; confirm patient and side; never give the diagnosis
core concept: Informed consent for an invasive procedure is obtained by the physician performing it and requires that the patient be competent, informed of the procedure's nature, its risks, benefits, and alternatives (including no procedure), and agree voluntarily. Consent is documented in writing, and a sonographer may serve as a witness. Before starting, a time-out following the Universal Protocol confirms the correct patient (two identifiers), procedure, side, and site, with the site marked when appropriate. Standard precautions, hand hygiene, sterile gloves, sterile gel, and sterile transducer covers are used for procedures, and transducers are cleaned and disinfected afterward according to manufacturer and facility protocol. Patient communication covers what to expect, how long it will take, comfort measures, and aftercare. Patient privacy is protected under HIPAA, and a chaperone may be offered. Sonographers describe the examination and its process but do not disclose diagnoses or interpretations; the interpreting physician communicates results. Anxious patients benefit from clear, calm explanations and the opportunity to ask questions.
why it matters: Many patient-care items test scope of practice. If a patient asks whether the mass is cancer, the correct response explains that the radiologist will review the images and the results will come from the physician, without false reassurance or speculation. Consent cannot be obtained from a sedated or confused patient, and it may be withdrawn at any time. A trap is thinking the sonographer obtains consent; the sonographer may witness it. Another trap is skipping the time-out for a simple procedure; every invasive procedure needs one.
on the registry: Expect scenarios about who obtains consent, the elements of informed consent, the purpose of a time-out, and how to respond when a patient asks for a diagnosis.
checkpoint: Physician consents, team times out, sonographer never diagnoses
